title: Delay engaging Drive or Reverse
h1: Why is there a delay when I shift into Drive or Reverse?
metaDesc: Car pauses before moving when you shift into Drive or Reverse? Answer a few questions to see if it's fluid, worn seals or a control problem, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: car takes a few seconds to go into gear
car wont move right away in drive
takes a while to go into drive
car hesitates to go into reverse
intro: Normally an automatic catches within a moment of shifting into Drive or Reverse. A pause of a second or more before the car moves means the transmission is slow to build the fluid pressure it needs. Answer a few questions to see the likely cause and how soon to act.
safety: Keep your foot firmly on the brake until the gear fully engages. Don't rev the engine to make it catch, because the car can lurch suddenly.
If the car won't engage at all, or you smell burning, don't keep trying. Have it towed.
Be extra careful backing out of parking spots or driveways while the delay is happening.

q_what.q: What happens after you shift into Drive or Reverse?

opts.a: It doesn't engage at all, or only moves if I rev the engine
There's also a burning smell, or red or pink fluid under the car
A pause only on the first drive of the day, then it's fine
A pause of a second or more every time, then it catches (maybe with a thud)

q_which.q: Is it slow to engage in Drive, Reverse, or both?

q_fluid.q: Have you been able to check the transmission fluid?
q_fluid.help: Many cars have a transmission dipstick, often with a yellow or red handle; others have none and must be checked by a shop. Your owner's manual explains how. Healthy fluid is usually red or pink and doesn't smell burnt.

opts.a: The level is OK, but it's dark brown or smells burnt
The level and color look normal
My car has no dipstick / I'm not sure
When the engine is hot, after driving a while
About the same whether hot or cold
It started right after a fluid change or battery work

result.title: The transmission may not be building enough pressure to drive the car
result.now: Put it in Park, turn the engine off and have the car towed. Don't rev the engine to force it into gear.
if: If there's red or pink fluid under the car, a major leak is the likely cause. Mention it when you call.
If the shifter moves but the gear display doesn't change, the shift cable or linkage may be broken. That's often a simpler repair.
If you smell burning or see smoke from under the car, step away. Transmission fluid on hot exhaust parts can catch fire.
result.why: When an automatic won't engage, or only catches after revving, it usually isn't getting enough fluid pressure to apply the clutches. Revving it can make the car lurch without warning and adds heat and wear to parts that are already slipping.

causes.name: Very low fluid from a leak
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the car, or a recent bump underneath.

causes.name: Failing transmission pump or badly worn internal parts
causes.clues: A whine that changes with engine speed, and a delay that got worse over weeks.

causes.name: Broken shift cable or linkage
causes.clues: The shifter feels loose, or the gear shown on the dash doesn't match the shifter.

you: From outside the car, look for red or pink fluid underneath.
Check whether the gear indicator on the dash matches the shifter position.

result.title: A transmission leak or overheating may be behind the delay
result.now: Don't use the car for now. Turn the engine off and have it towed.
if: If you see smoke, step away from the car. Fluid dripping on the exhaust can catch fire.
If it's only a few drops and there's no burning smell, check the fluid level once the car is cool, but still have it inspected before driving it.
If a transmission temperature warning came on, tell the shop when you call.
result.why: The transmission needs a full supply of fluid to build pressure quickly when you select a gear. A leak lets the level drop, which causes the delay, and a burning smell means fluid or parts are overheating.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket, cooler line or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink fluid under the middle or front of the car.

causes.name: Overheating from internal slipping
causes.clues: A sharp burnt smell after driving.

causes.name: Fluid dripping onto the exhaust
causes.clues: Smoke from under the car along with the leak.

you: Note the color of any fluid under the car.

result.title: A first-start delay can mean fluid is draining back overnight
result.now: After starting, wait a few seconds with your foot on the brake before shifting, and book a transmission check when convenient.
if: If the delay gets longer or starts happening after short stops too, get it checked within a few days.
If you find the fluid low, top it up with the correct type and have the leak found within a few days. Low fluid usually means it's escaping somewhere.
If you smell burning, the car lurches into gear, or it slips while driving, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: When a car sits overnight, some fluid can drain out of the torque converter and passages, especially past worn seals. The transmission then needs a moment to refill and build pressure before the gear catches. It's an early warning sign worth catching before it gets worse.

causes.name: Fluid draining out of the torque converter or passages
causes.clues: Only after sitting for hours, and fine for the rest of the day.

causes.name: Hardened or worn internal seals
causes.clues: Older or high-mileage car, and worse in cold weather.

causes.name: Slightly low fluid
causes.clues: A small leak, or a level at the low mark.

you: Time the delay on a few mornings so you can tell if it's getting worse.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.

result.title: A delay only in Reverse can point to a worn reverse clutch, band or seals
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days. Until then, hold the brake firmly until Reverse fully engages before backing up.
if: If Reverse stops engaging at all, don't keep trying. Have it checked before using the car.
If the fluid is low, top it up with the correct type and have the leak found. Low fluid often shows up in Reverse first.
If you smell burning or the car lurches backward when Reverse catches, stop using it and have it checked.
result.why: Reverse uses its own clutch or band inside the transmission, and it often needs more pressure than Drive. When that part or its seals start to wear, or the fluid is a little low, Reverse is often the first gear to show a delay. A shop will usually check the fluid, codes and pressure before recommending internal repairs.

causes.name: Worn reverse clutch, band or seals
causes.clues: High mileage, and the delay in Reverse is slowly getting longer.

causes.name: Low fluid
causes.clues: Red or pink drips, or a level below the mark.

causes.name: Sticking valve or solenoid
causes.clues: The delay comes and goes, sometimes with a check engine light.

you: Check the fluid level if your car has a dipstick.
Time the delay so you can tell if it's getting worse.

result.title: Low transmission fluid may be causing the delay, and it's likely leaking somewhere
result.now: Top up with the exact fluid type listed in your owner's manual, then have the leak found within the next few days.
if: If the delay continues after topping up, keep trips short and get it checked sooner.
If the level drops again quickly or you see fluid dripping, stop using the car until the leak is fixed.
If you see smoke or smell burning fluid, turn the engine off and step away. Fluid on the exhaust can catch fire.
result.why: With low fluid, the transmission pump has to work harder to build pressure, so there's a pause before the gear catches. Fluid doesn't get used up in normal driving, so a low level usually means a leak, even if you can't see drips.

causes.name: Leaking pan gasket or seal
causes.clues: Red or pink drips under the middle of the car.

causes.name: Leaking cooler line
causes.clues: Drips near the front of the car, under the radiator.

causes.name: Level set too low at a recent service
causes.clues: The delay started soon after a fluid change.

you: Recheck the level after a few days.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to spot drips.
shop: Correct fluid level check to factory procedure

result.title: Worn or overheated fluid, possibly with internal wear
result.now: Have the transmission inspected within the next few days and ask whether a fluid service is right for its condition.
if: If the shop finds metal debris in the pan, a deeper repair may be needed rather than just new fluid. Ask them to show you what they found.
If the delay gets much longer or it starts slipping, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a transmission temperature warning comes on or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: Dark, burnt-smelling fluid has been overheated and no longer protects or seals as well. That can slow how quickly gears engage, and it often means parts inside have been working harder than they should.

causes.name: Overdue fluid service
causes.clues: No record of a fluid change, especially with towing or heavy use.

causes.name: Worn internal seals or clutches
causes.clues: High mileage, and the delay is slowly getting longer.

causes.name: Past overheating
causes.clues: A history of towing, mountain driving or a transmission temperature warning.

you: Find your records of the last transmission fluid service.

result.title: A delay that's worse when hot can point to internal wear leaking pressure
result.now: Have the transmission checked within the next few days, and avoid towing or long hot drives until then.
if: If a transmission temperature warning comes on or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
If it starts slipping while driving, get it checked right away.
result.why: Hot fluid is thinner, so it escapes more easily past worn seals and a worn pump. That lowers pressure when you select a gear, causing a pause. The problem usually grows as the wear continues. A shop will usually do a pressure test hot and cold before deciding on a repair.

causes.name: Worn transmission pump
causes.clues: A whine that rises with engine speed.

causes.name: Worn internal seals
causes.clues: High mileage, and fine when cold.

causes.name: Worn or overheated fluid
causes.clues: Dark fluid or a burnt smell.

you: Note how long you'd been driving when the delay was worst.
shop: Line pressure test hot and cold

result.title: A steady delay with normal fluid may point to a pressure control or internal problem
result.now: Have the codes read and the transmission checked within the next few days.
if: If the delay gets longer or it starts slipping, stop driving it and have it towed.
If a code points to a solenoid or sensor, the repair may be smaller than a rebuild.
If you smell burning or a transmission temperature warning comes on, stop driving it and have it towed.
result.why: If the fluid is full and clean but the delay happens every time, the problem may be in how pressure is controlled or held. A shop will usually scan for codes and test pressure and solenoids before recommending a rebuild. That can be an electronic solenoid, a sticking valve, or wear to seals and clutches.

causes.name: Faulty pressure control solenoid
causes.clues: A check engine light, or harsh shifts as well.

causes.name: Sticking valve in the valve body
causes.clues: The delay varies from one day to the next.

causes.name: Worn seals or clutches
causes.clues: High mileage and a delay that's slowly getting longer.

you: Time the delay in Drive and Reverse.

result.title: A delay that started after service may be a fluid level, fluid type or relearn issue
result.now: Check the service invoice for the fluid type used, and ask the shop that did the work to recheck the level.
if: If the wrong fluid was used, have it corrected soon. The wrong type can cause delays and harsh shifts.
If it started after battery work and is improving day by day, the transmission may be relearning. Book a check if it hasn't settled after about a week.
If the delay is getting worse, it slips, or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it checked.
result.why: Transmission fluid levels must be set using a specific procedure, often with the engine warm. An incorrect level, the wrong fluid, or learned settings wiped by a battery disconnect can all cause a delay into gear.

causes.name: Fluid level set wrong
causes.clues: The delay started right after a fluid change.

causes.name: Wrong fluid type
causes.clues: The invoice lists a fluid not named in your owner's manual.

causes.name: Shift adaptations reset after battery work
causes.clues: It started after battery work and is slowly improving.

you: Compare the fluid on the invoice with your owner's manual.
shop: Fluid level check to factory procedure
Transmission adaptation relearn with a scan tool

result.title: Have the transmission checked before the delay gets longer
result.now: Book a transmission check within the next week or two. Time the delay in Drive and Reverse so you can tell the shop.
if: If the delay grows quickly, it starts slipping, or you smell burning, stop driving it and have it towed.
If you can check the fluid and it's low, top it up with the correct type and look for a leak.
result.why: Delayed engagement means the transmission is slow to build pressure. It's often an early sign of low fluid or wear that's cheaper to deal with now than later.

causes.name: Low or worn fluid
causes.clues: Drips under the car or no record of a fluid service.

causes.name: Worn internal seals
causes.clues: Worse on cold mornings or when hot.

causes.name: Pressure control fault
causes.clues: A warning light or harsh shifts too.

you: Time the delay in Drive and Reverse.
Look for red or pink drips where you park.
